clue.text: Going round knocking back shots, initially neat gin, getting sozzled

indicators.note: knocking back drinks suggests tipping them backwards, so the word for shots is read in reverse

parts.note: nips are small shots of spirits

indicators.note: initially says take only the opening letter of the next word

parts.note: first letter of neat

indicators.note: sozzled means drunk, so the letters of gin stagger into a new order

explanation.surface: A drinker's head is going round after downing shots and neat gin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocking back' turns NIPS into SPIN; then N (first of 'neat') and 'sozzled' rearranges GIN to ING.
explanation.definitionFit: Something spinning is rotating, turning on its axis, which is what going round means.

clue.text: Very brilliant boss of newspaper, although it's folding

parts.note: so means very, as in 'so good'
fab is slang for fabulous, brilliant
the editor runs a newspaper, abbreviated ED

explanation.surface: A newspaper editor is praised as brilliant even though the paper is closing down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'folding' seems to mean a paper going out of business; it is furniture that folds out into a bed.
explanation.definitionFit: A sofa bed is a couch whose frame unfolds into a bed for sleeping.

clue.text: Lee Dixon originally turned up bearing sign of rustiness

indicators.note: turned up says the hidden letters are read backwards
bearing means carrying, so the phrase before it carries the answer within its letters

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A veteran footballer, Lee Dixon, first showed up looking a bit rusty.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'bearing sign of rustiness' as the definition, but 'bearing' is the signal that the reversed phrase carries the answer; the definition is just 'sign of rustiness'. Lee Dixon is a former Arsenal defender.
explanation.definitionFit: Rust is the reddish compound formed when iron reacts with oxygen and water, so it visibly shows corrosion.

clue.text: Last of Buster Keaton's reels — zero interest

indicators.note: reels means staggers, so the letters lurch into a new order
last of means only the final letter of the following word

parts.note: taken as written; its final letter is used
taken as written

explanation.surface: Nobody wants Buster Keaton's last silent-film reels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reels' looks like film reels; it is the verb, to stagger.
explanation.definitionFit: If there are no takers for an offer, nobody accepts it: no one is interested.

clue.text: User of products from top line machine might have these uncomfortable feelings when cycling

definitions.text: User of products from top line machine might have these uncomfortable feelings when cycling

parts.words: User of products from top line machine might have these uncomfortable feelings when cycling
parts.note: the grid's top line spells a famous cotton-spinning machine, whose thread a sewer uses with these; and the phrase for tingling limbs, words cycled round, gives the answer

explanation.walkthrough: The top row of the grid reads SPINNING JENNY, the cotton-spinning machine; someone sewing with its thread uses needles and pins. Cycling the words of 'pins and needles', the tingling feeling, gives the same phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Sewing uses needles for stitching and pins for holding fabric; 'pins and needles' is the prickling sensation in a limb.

clue.text: 2002 record catch supplied by Scotsman, according to Spooner

indicators.note: Spooner, the Oxford don famed for swapping initial sounds, signals that the opening sounds of the two key words change places

parts.note: a blenny is a small fish, something an angler might catch
something supplied by a person comes from the person
Jock is a familiar name for a Scotsman

explanation.surface: A fish catch handed over by a Scot, told in the reverend Spooner's muddled style.
explanation.walkthrough: BLENNY FROM THE JOCK swaps its opening sounds BL and J to give the title of Jennifer Lopez's 2002 hit.
explanation.definitionFit: Jenny from the Block is a 2002 single by Jennifer Lopez, so it is a record from that year.

clue.text: Texan oilman embracing the poor old priest

indicators.note: embracing means holding inside, so the oilman's initials surround the rest

parts.note: J R Ewing is the Texan oil baron in the TV soap Dallas

indicators.note: poor means shoddy, badly made, so the letters of the are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A Texan oil tycoon hugs a poor elderly priest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poor' rearranges THE to ETH, which sits between J and R; O for 'old' follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Jethro was the Midianite priest in Exodus whose daughter married Moses.

clue.text: Piece of Bellini, Mendelssohn or Massenet screened

indicators.note: screened means concealed, so the answer lies hidden in the composers' names

explanation.surface: A concert programme screened works by Bellini, Mendelssohn or Massenet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'screened' sounds like a broadcast; here it means hidden.
explanation.definitionFit: Norma is Bellini's 1831 opera, a famous work from that Italian composer.

clue.text: Men with baseball bats force Kanye West to get undressed

indicators.note: force means wrench out of shape, so the letters of Kanye are pushed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: undressed means stripped of outer layers, so West loses its first and last letters

parts.note: taken as written; only its middle letters are used

explanation.surface: Baseball players with bats make the rapper Kanye West strip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'force' rearranges KANYE to YANKE; 'undressed' strips West to ES.
explanation.definitionFit: The New York Yankees are a famous baseball team, so their players carry baseball bats.

clue.text: Have mixed feelings about black/blue markings on taps

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
low means blue, in the sense of down or depressed
taps are labelled hot and cold

explanation.surface: Wondering about the black-and-blue labels on bathroom taps.
explanation.definitionFit: To blow hot and cold is an idiom for vacillating, being keen one moment and cool the next.

clue.text: See 5
Subsequently, Tinseltown star Charlize dumps husband

parts.note: Tinseltown is a nickname for Hollywood, in Los Angeles, abbreviated LA

indicators.note: dumps means gets rid of, so the husband's letter is dropped from the star's surname

parts.note: Charlize Theron is a Hollywood film star

explanation.surface: Gossip-column news: a Hollywood actress has left her husband.
explanation.definitionFit: Later on means at a later time, afterwards, a direct synonym of subsequently.

clue.text: See 5
empty luggage rack like this?

parts.note: taking a bag down from a rack lowers the case; and the clue itself is printed in small letters, starting with uncapitalised 'empty'

explanation.walkthrough: The clue begins without a capital letter, a deliberate hint: the whole clue is written in small letters, and emptying a rack means lowering each case.
explanation.definitionFit: Lower case is the printing term for small letters, as opposed to capitals, which is how this clue is set.

clue.text: Victor left golf club as the rain eased off

indicators.note: left here means departed, so the letter for Victor goes out of the club

parts.note: a driver is the golf club used for long tee shots
Victor is V in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A golfer called Victor walked out of the clubhouse once the rain had stopped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'golf club' looks like a clubhouse Victor walked out of; it is the club in the bag, the DRIVER.
explanation.definitionFit: When rain eases off, conditions become less wet, and the comparative for that is drier.

clue.text: Layabout seen in Salcombe every now and again

indicators.note: every now and again means taking letters at intervals, here the first, third, fifth and seventh

parts.note: a seaside town in Devon, England

explanation.surface: A lazy person is spotted occasionally in the Devon resort of Salcombe.
explanation.definitionFit: A slob is a lazy, untidy person, much the same as an idle layabout.

clue.text: First signs of law and order stabilised the country

indicators.note: first signs means the opening letter of each word that follows

explanation.surface: The return of law and order steadied the nation.
explanation.definitionFit: Laos is a landlocked nation in Southeast Asia, bordering Vietnam and Thailand.

clue.text: A commercial vehicle transporting a large red slide

indicators.note: transporting means carrying, so the van holds A and L inside it

parts.note: a van is a goods vehicle used by businesses
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
Che Guevara, the revolutionary, is a byword for a red, a communist

explanation.surface: A delivery van carries a big red playground slide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slide' looks like playground equipment; it is a fall of snow down a mountain.
explanation.definitionFit: An avalanche is a mass of snow sliding down a mountainside, so a slide in that sense.

clue.text: Book July to go off with Mick

indicators.note: to go off means to explode or go bad, so the letters are blown apart and reassembled

explanation.surface: Booking a July trip away with someone called Mick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book' looks like a verb, to reserve; it is a noun, the novel by Kingsley Amis.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucky Jim is Kingsley Amis's 1954 comic novel, so it is a book.

clue.text: A revolting expression of indifference used to attract attention

indicators.note: revolting is read as turning over, so the indifferent word is flipped backwards

parts.note: meh is a modern interjection of boredom or indifference

explanation.surface: A disgusting 'whatever' is uttered to make people notice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolting' looks like disgusting but signals turning MEH around to HEM.
explanation.definitionFit: Ahem is the little throat-clearing noise people make to catch someone's notice.

clue.text: Dying to hear part of National Lear soliloquy

indicators.note: part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Theatre-goers eager to hear a speech from the National Theatre's King Lear.
explanation.definitionFit: Being all ears is an idiom for listening eagerly, keen to know something.

clue.text: Old Peruvian picking edges off tiny scab

indicators.note: picking off the edges removes each word's first and last letters, keeping the inside

explanation.surface: Someone picks at the edges of a little scab.
explanation.definitionFit: The Incas were the people of the pre-Columbian empire centred on Peru.

clue.text: 1A mum ran upstairs, about to confiscate a weapon

indicators.note: the answer to 1 across means going round, so the hidden letters are turned to read backwards
about here means around or within, so the answer is found inside these words

parts.note: the letters run from the end of mum, through ran, into the start of upstairs

explanation.surface: A mother dashes upstairs, intending to take a weapon off a child.
explanation.walkthrough: '1A' stands for SPINNING, the answer to 1 across, used here as the signal to read the hidden letters backwards. 'about' signals the hidden run MRANU.
explanation.definitionFit: To unarm is an old verb for disarm, to strip someone of weapons.

clue.text: Lazy siesta beneath the cover of Monsieur Henri?

indicators.note: in a down answer, beneath puts the rearranged siesta after the M
a cover sits on top, so take the first letter of the following word

parts.note: taken as written; its first letter is used

indicators.note: lazy letters lie about loosely, so siesta is rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A Frenchman called Henri takes a lazy afternoon nap under the covers.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that Henri is an example: Henri Matisse.
explanation.definitionFit: Henri Matisse was the French painter; the forename stands for him as an example.

clue.text: Save money on second hairstyle

indicators.note: in a down answer, on means placed above, so S sits on top of the rest

parts.note: a crimp is hair pressed into small waves

explanation.surface: Cutting costs on a second visit to the hairdresser.
explanation.definitionFit: To scrimp is to be frugal, economising carefully on spending.

clue.text: Excited handclap welcomes United — ground expecting explosive start!

indicators.note: welcomes means takes in, so the U goes inside the rearranged letters
excited letters are agitated and stirred up into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
U is a common abbreviation for United in team names

explanation.surface: Applause greets a football team called United at a stadium awaiting a lively kick-off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ground' looks like a football stadium; it is the patch of ground a rocket blasts off from.
explanation.definitionFit: A launch pad is the platform from which a rocket lifts off with an explosive ignition.

clue.text: Occasionally funny caller (relatively speaking!)

indicators.note: occasionally means now and then, so take every other letter, the second, fourth and so on

explanation.surface: A sometimes amusing visitor, who turns out to be a family member.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket tells us this caller is a relative, which is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An uncle is a family relation, a parent's brother, so he is one speaking in relative terms.

clue.text: Wrapping prow of Kon-Tiki (Heyerdahl's vessel)

indicators.note: the prow is the front of a boat, so take the front letter

parts.note: Kon-Tiki was Thor Heyerdahl's balsa raft
Thor Heyerdahl sailed the Pacific on a raft

explanation.surface: Describing the front of Thor Heyerdahl's famous ocean-crossing raft.
explanation.definitionFit: Kraft is strong brown paper used for wrapping parcels.

clue.text: Where to sell gold coin crooked tenor smuggled?

parts.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold

indicators.note: smuggled means slipped in secretly, so the T is hidden inside
crooked means bent, so the letters of coin are twisted out of order

parts.note: taken as written
T is a standard abbreviation for tenor in music

explanation.surface: Asking where to fence a gold coin that a dishonest singer smuggled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crooked' rearranges COIN to CION, and 'smuggled' puts T inside it to give CTION after AU.
explanation.definitionFit: An auction is a sale where goods go to the highest bidder, a place to sell things.

clue.text: Protests over British planes storing up carbon

parts.note: O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over

indicators.note: storing up means holding inside, so carbon is tucked within the planes

parts.note: jets are jet-engined aircraft
C is the chemical symbol for carbon

explanation.surface: Environmental protests about British aircraft building up carbon emissions.
explanation.definitionFit: To object is to raise an objection or complain, so objects is the verb for protests.

clue.text: Demanding pace needs an injection of energy

indicators.note: an injection puts something inside, so the E goes into the step

parts.note: a pace is a step
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A runner's tiring pace calls for an energy boost.
explanation.definitionFit: A steep price or request is excessive, making heavy demands, so steep can mean demanding.

clue.text: American lady acquiring book, edited novel by Eliot

indicators.note: acquiring means taking in, so book and edited go inside the lady

parts.note: a dame is a titled lady

explanation.surface: An American woman buys a book, an edited copy of George Eliot's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: George Eliot, not T S Eliot, is the novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Adam Bede (1859) was the first full-length novel by George Eliot, the Victorian writer.
